Agent platform eval

This report is a controls comparison of three ways to run a Claude agent on an issue: two of them run Claude Code, and the third runs the Managed Agents harness. The experiment ran to settle the direction of dotnet-software-factory v2.

Source: the repo. Design and status: the plan.

How to read it

Cloud Sessions is a VM that Anthropic manages. The platform is the factory at v1.1.0 in Docker, on a self-hosted runner in a lab VM. Both arms ran the same agent on the same model, claude-sonnet-5-5. They ran against one target repo, sbiondolillo/platform-eval-sample. Issue #1 is the delivery, and issue #2 is the probes.

A probe run in the real product proves every Cloud cell. A public asset proves every platform cell. Each cell links its proof.

The platform arm is a homelab: one runner host, a Squid proxy, a self-hosted vault and a self-hosted gateway. It stands in for an enterprise platform and is not one. The product fixes the Cloud cells. The platform cells are a floor. Where an enterprise component would change a row, the platform cell carries a footnote. The footnote says what changes.

The third arm, Managed Agents, was added on 2026-10-27. The Managed Agents docs prove its cells. Where the docs are silent, one session proves the cell. Managed Agents is the vendor's product. So, like the Cloud cells, the product fixes its cells.

The controls

rowCloud SessionsPlatformManaged Agents
cloud-logging Cloud Sessions keep the error text in the server-side transcript, readable by signed-in accounts through the web UI, the Share link and the CLI; nothing is exported to disk. the GitHub job log holds the 403 line and the stack trace for 90 days, readable by any signed-in GitHub account, and the gateway ledger holds the run's calls and spend but not the failure. the stderr of a failed command is in the session's agent.tool_result event, read by API with the workspace key, without the exit code.
substrate the agent runs as root with cap_sys_admin inside its own Firecracker microVM, so the VM boundary is the whole isolation. the agent runs as an unprivileged uid with Docker's default capabilities in a container that shares the runner VM's kernel, so the container and the VM are two boundaries, and the factory sets none of the container's confinement itself.1 the agent runs as root with cap_sys_admin in a Docker container inside a Firecracker microVM, under a harness that is not Claude Code, and the environment carries a commit-signing token the docs do not name.
model-credential the VM holds the account's OAuth token in a file that the root agent can read, and model calls skip the egress proxy, so the credential that the agent can read has the reach of the whole account. the container holds only a lab gateway key, usable from inside the lab and logged per call, and the vendor key never enters the Sandbox VLAN, but the gateway sets no budget or model list on that key.2 the sandbox holds no model key, because the service makes the model call, but it holds a 61-character commit-signing token whose reach was not probed.
forge-credential the sandbox holds no token on disk, but the managed proxy injects the operator's own account credential with admin on the one granted repo, scoped away from the owner's other repos until add_repo is called. the agent's container holds no forge credential at all; the operator's fine-grained PAT and a job-scoped Actions token both sit in the factory process on the host, and the pull request is opened under the operator account.3 the sandbox holds no forge token on disk or in its environment; a credential helper injects whatever token the caller passed, so a read-only token gives fetch and a 403 on push, and the identity on the forge is the token's.
vault-secret the managed proxy attaches the secret on the way out and only to its allowed hosts, so the agent's VM never holds a value it can read. infisical run puts the secret in the runner job's environment, so the factory process can read it and must attach it itself, and the agent's container gets it only when the factory passes it by name.4 the docs put the value on the egress path for the credential's listed hosts, with a placeholder in the sandbox; the vault and the binding were accepted, and the one-request test was refused by the model-side safeguard.
egress a local relay tunnels HTTPS only to exact allowed hostnames on port 443, and the gateway intercepts every direct port 443 connection and answers it itself, so no request reaches the internet except through the relay. Squid tunnels only to the hosts on the runner's per-source allowlist, which the operator edits by hand, and the firewall drops every direct connection, so Squid is the only path out.5 an unlisted hostname does not resolve and a raw IP meets a foreign certificate, so allowed_hosts on the environment is the whole egress control, except that api.anthropic.com answers from any sandbox.
tool-model-policy the operator picks any of twelve models with no control and the account's connectors set the tools, so the only controls observed were the egress relay, the start-time tool loading and a model-side safeguard that acts on prompt content. the factory fixes the model and the tools in code and Squid stops a new remote server, but the agent holds a gateway key with no model list and runs with every tool allowed, so it can call any gateway model on its own.6 the agent's model pin is a default that any agent_with_overrides create body replaces, so the control on model and tools is whoever holds the API key, and the sandbox holds none.
run-history sessions are listed and read only inside the product, in the web UI, the Share link, claude --teleport and the in-session MCP tools, and no documented API or CLI command lists them or exports a transcript to a file. gh lists the runs and downloads the 90-day job log, the gateway ledger holds every model call, and the model transcripts are files that the v1.2.1 starter pushes to a private store repo, but this target repo's v1.1.0 workflow has no store step, so they stay on the runner host only until the next run.7 GET /v1/sessions lists sessions by agent with their metadata and cost, and GET /v1/sessions/{id}/events exports the whole transcript, so every capture of this arm came out by API.
spend-attribution with the collector host on the environment's Allowed domains, the environment-variables route lands the cost metric and the token counts in the operator's Grafana keyed by ccr_session_id. Four earlier sessions with the host only on a network secret exported nothing, since the telemetry export never gets a secret's host exception. with a nine-name pass-through in the factory, the cost metric and one event per API request land in the operator's Grafana keyed by session id, and the metric reads within one export interval of the factory's own log.8 usage.list_cost per session, with the caller's metadata on it, gives the cost of one review keyed by pull request from a list call, and a telemetry destination in the Console sends every session's spans with token counts to Grafana Cloud with no export from the sandbox or the job.
audit-record the in-VM transcript is root-writable and only the auto-mode classifier stopped an append and a delete, so the record a compromised agent cannot erase is the server-side transcript outside the VM. the agent can edit or delete its own transcript on the runner with no control, so the records it cannot erase are the host-written job log, pull request history and the gateway's per-call ledger.9 the session's events live outside the sandbox and are read by the API key the sandbox does not hold, and the model-side safeguard refused the sweep that would have tested an in-sandbox route to them.
github-start a label can start a Cloud session, but only through a GitHub job that the repo owner writes and that holds a per-task bearer token, and the session's reply stays at claude.ai/code unless the prompt posts it back. the factory label starts the delivery run on the self-hosted runner directly through the workflow's issues: labeled trigger, gated to the repo owner, with no start credential. a workflow job starts a session with a workspace API key held as a repository secret, with no trigger in the product and no idempotency key, so the job dedupes and orchestrates.
crash-resume the Stop button loses nothing, and an idle reclaim keeps the disk and the history and kills every process, so a session resumes on its own files. a factory job has no resume; the container is removed at job end and only the pushed branch, the pull request and the saved transcript remain. an idle sandbox is checkpointed, and a message 21 minutes later resumed it on a fresh boot with the files intact and every process gone, the same as the Cloud arm's idle reclaim.
subagent-record the subagent keeps its own transcript in the VM's session folder, and the server-side transcript keeps its report and a row with its model, but whether the subagent's own transcript outlives the container is pending the reclaim step. the subagent's transcript lands beside the parent's on the runner host until the next job, it is never uploaded without the v1.2.1 store step, and the gateway ledger counts its calls under dsf with no link to the parent.10 there is no subagent; each reviewer is its own session with its own server-side record, and the job is the fan-out.
toolchain a setup script in the environment installs the SDK once, and later sessions start from a filesystem snapshot that the docs say is rebuilt on a script or allowlist change and after about seven days, but the UI shows no setup duration. the factory builds a 2.11 GB image from its own Dockerfile on the runner host at first use in about 66 s, each job then pays about 16 s of toolchain setup, and the image never expires and changes only when someone deletes it.11 packages installs the Ubuntu archive's dotnet-sdk-10.0, which is 10.0.113, in a first session of 53 active seconds, and the target's 10.0.4xx band needs a route the docs do not give.
branch-protection the session pushed to protected main and the push landed as an administrator bypass, because the proxy pushes as the operator's admin account and the protection lets administrators bypass, so the protection does not bind the agent. the factory's source pushes only its own branch and opens a pull request, so the required checks apply at the merge, but the PAT is on the same admin account and the protection would not stop a direct push. the sandbox's token cannot push at all, and the judge reaches the pull request as a check run through the job's own scoped token, which branch protection can require.
setup-cost Cloud Sessions took 25 operator steps and 4 secrets, all in web forms, GitHub and the workstation, with 8 steps and no secret to reach the first pull request and no lab host touched. the platform took 28 operator steps and no new secret in the experiment, on top of 9 lab items and 4 secrets that the lab already held, and it touched 3 lab hosts in the experiment and 6 with its prerequisites.12 6 operator steps and 2 new secrets from zero to the first posted review, with none of the platform arm's 9 lab items.

Footnotes: what an enterprise component changes

Rows without a footnote are set by GitHub or by the factory's own design, not by a lab stand-in.

  1. substrate. The lab runs the container on one shared runner VM, with Docker's default capabilities. A platform with one VM per job, or with a sandboxed runtime, gives each job its own boundary. back
  2. model-credential. The lab gateway issues one static consumer key, with no budget and no model list. A gateway that issues a per-job key with a budget and a model list ends the key's reach with the job. back
  3. forge-credential. The lab uses the operator's fine-grained PAT, and the factory process reads it from the vault. A GitHub App, or a vault that issues a short-lived installation token per job, lets the factory open the pull request under a bot identity. back
  4. vault-secret. The lab's infisical run step puts the secret in the job's environment, and Squid tunnels TLS by host only. A vault agent or a TLS-terminating proxy attaches the secret per request and binds it to a host. Then the factory process never holds the value, as in the Cloud cell. back
  5. egress. Squid tunnels by host, and the operator edits the allowlist by hand. A TLS-terminating proxy inspects the path and the method, and a managed allowlist replaces the hand edit. The host-only rule stays the floor. back
  6. tool-model-policy. The factory's code holds the model pin, and the gateway key has no model list. A model list on the key moves the pin into the gateway, where the agent cannot change it. Squid still stops a new remote server by host only. back
  7. run-history. The transcripts stay on the runner host until the next run, and the ledger is a lab ClickHouse table. An artifact store, or the store step of the v1.2.1 starter, keeps the transcripts past the next run. An enterprise gateway's own ledger replaces the lab table. back
  8. spend-attribution. The lab's cost metric needs a nine-name pass-through in the factory. A per-job key attributes spend on the gateway ledger with no pass-through. The OpenTelemetry route stays as a second readout. back
  9. audit-record. The agent can edit its own transcript on the runner host. A transcript upload at job end, or a log sink that the agent cannot reach, adds a record that the agent cannot edit. The job log and the ledger are the floor. back
  10. subagent-record. The subagent's transcript stays on the runner host until the next job. The store step or the artifact store from the run-history row keeps it too. A per-job key separates its calls from the parent's calls on the ledger. back
  11. toolchain. The lab builds the image on the runner host, and the image never expires. An image registry with a rebuild schedule gives the platform the rebuild that Cloud Sessions does on its own. back
  12. setup-cost. The lab already held 9 items and 4 secrets before the experiment. In an enterprise, the platform team does that work. So the factory owner's count is the 28 steps alone. back

The conditional

A verdict hides the rows that are the same under either choice. Read the conditional cell by cell.

Rows Cloud Sessions covers today

  • cloud-logging: the server-side transcript keeps the error text for signed-in accounts.
  • substrate: each session runs in its own Firecracker microVM.
  • vault-secret: the managed proxy attaches the secret on the way out, so the VM never holds a value it can read.
  • egress: a local relay tunnels HTTPS only to exact allowed hostnames. The platform covers this row too, with a hand-edited allowlist.
  • audit-record: the server-side transcript outside the VM is a record that a compromised agent cannot erase.
  • github-start: a label can start a Cloud session, through a glue job that the repo owner writes.
  • crash-resume: an idle reclaim keeps the disk and the history, so a session resumes on its own files.
  • toolchain: a setup script installs the SDK once, and later sessions start from a filesystem snapshot.

Rows the factory owner must build under either choice

Both arms act under the operator's admin account. So a non-admin identity and a protection with no bypass are build items, whichever arm wins.

  • forge-credential: the Cloud proxy injects the operator's own admin credential, and the platform's PAT is on the same admin account.
  • branch-protection: the Cloud session pushed to protected main as an admin bypass, and the protection would not stop a direct push from the platform's PAT.

Rows only the platform can hold

  • model-credential: on Cloud Sessions the agent can read the account's OAuth token. The platform container holds only a gateway key, and the platform owes a budget on that key.
  • tool-model-policy: on Cloud Sessions the operator picks any of twelve models with no control. The platform fixes the model in code, and owes a model list on the gateway key.

Rows the docs do not settle, with the probe result

  • run-history: no documented API or CLI command lists Cloud sessions or exports a transcript.
  • spend-attribution: Cloud lands the cost metric keyed by ccr.session.id once the collector host is on the environment's Allowed domains. Four earlier sessions exported nothing with the host only on a network secret. The platform lands it with a nine-name pass-through.
  • subagent-record: whether the subagent's own transcript outlives the container is pending the reclaim step.

setup-cost: Cloud Sessions took 25 operator steps and 4 secrets. The platform took 28 steps and no new secret, on top of 9 lab items and 4 secrets that the lab already held.

What the third arm changes

Managed Agents fills the same rows. It moves some rows into the product and leaves others with the owner.

Rows Managed Agents covers today

  • cloud-logging: the stderr of a failed command is in the session's events, read by API.
  • substrate: the agent runs as root in a Docker container inside a Firecracker microVM.
  • model-credential: the sandbox holds no model key, because the service makes the call. A commit-signing token is present, and its reach is not probed.
  • forge-credential: a credential helper injects the caller's token per request. So a read-only token gives fetch and a 403 on push.
  • egress: an unlisted hostname does not resolve. But api.anthropic.com answers from any sandbox.
  • run-history: the list and events endpoints export every session and its whole transcript.
  • spend-attribution: the API gives each session's list_cost with its metadata. A Console telemetry destination landed a session trace in Grafana Cloud.
  • audit-record: the events live outside the sandbox, read by a key the sandbox does not hold. The safeguard refused the in-sandbox route.
  • crash-resume: an idle sandbox is checkpointed. A later message resumes it with the files kept and the processes gone.
  • github-start: a workflow job starts a session with a workspace API key. The product has no idempotency key.
  • subagent-record: there is no subagent. Each reviewer is its own session with its own record.

Rows the owner must build on Managed Agents

  • tool-model-policy: the agent's model pin is a default that any create body overrides. So the control is whoever holds the API key.
  • branch-protection: require the judge check run. The session's token cannot push.
  • vault-secret: the docs are the only proof. The model-side safeguard refused the one-request test twice.
  • toolchain: the apt SDK is 10.0.113, and the target's band is 10.0.4xx. So the mutation angle stays on the runner.

setup-cost: Managed Agents took 6 operator steps and 2 new secrets. Cloud Sessions took 25 steps and 4 secrets. The platform took 28 steps and no new secret, on 9 lab items.

One rung per arm

A trust ladder grades the phases of one change: issue, plan, build, review, feedback, deliver and merge. Each rung up hands one phase from a person to an agent or to code.

  • Rung 0: every phase is a person.
  • Rung 1: plan and build are an agent. Review is an agent plus a person. Deliver is code.
  • Rung 2: feedback is an agent that answers its own review threads.
  • Rung 3: the issue is an agent.
  • Rung 4: the review loses its person.
  • Rung 5: merge is code.

Two lines hold at every rung. Deliver is code. The agent never holds the credential that opens the pull request.

Platform: rung 2

The factory's source pushes the branch and opens the pull request. The agent's container holds no forge credential. The review is an agent gate, with a person at the merge.

Proof: forge-credential, platform-delivery.

Cloud Sessions: below rung 1

The agent itself pushed the branch and opened PR 5. It did this through the managed proxy, with the operator's admin credential. In the branch-protection probe, it pushed to protected main. Deliver is the agent, not code.

Rung 1 needs a deliver step outside the session and a non-admin identity. The glue job from the github-start row is the place to build it.

Proof: forge-credential, branch-protection, github-start.

Managed Agents: rung 1, both lines held by the product

A Claude Code session built the subject. Two Managed Agents sessions reviewed it, with a person at the merge. Deliver is code. The workflow job posts the review and the check run with its own scoped token. The agent never holds the credential that opens or merges a pull request. The session's token is read-only, and the product's helper injects it.

Proof: forge-credential, branch-protection, platform-delivery.
